steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper evaluating how well GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and a fine-tuned Llama-2-7b can formulate mathematical optimization problems from natural language descriptions. Motivate the problem, give NLP/LLM background, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Optimization problems are everywhere, but formulating them needs expertise
- Automating formulation would make optimization accessible
- NLP and LLM progress
- Gap: no formal assessment of GPT-3.5/GPT-4 on this task; fine-tuning a smaller LLM
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Optimization and the expertise barrier
  - practical challenges from operations, economics, engineering, computer science -> optimization problems (cite)
  - standard algorithms solve them efficiently: simplex (cite), interior-point (cite)
  - translating a real-world situation into a mathematical formulation needs specialized knowledge
  - barrier keeps many people from using optimization even when it would help
- Automating formulation
  - natural language description -> decision variables, constraints, objective
  - accessible beyond operations research experts; for those who cannot afford experts
  - once correctly formulated, transcribe into algebraic modeling language for solvers (cite)
- NLP / LLMs
  - NLP: potent avenue for accessible, efficient formulation
  - word embeddings -> language models, transformative progress
  - pre-trained language models (cite): state of the art on NLI, QA, summarization, collaborative writing, minimal task-specific fine-tuning (cite)
  - recent LLMs: GPT (cite), Llama (cite) reshaped NLP
  - billions to hundreds of billions of parameters; zero-shot / few-shot generalization via prompting
  - strong fine-tuning even on much smaller datasets than predecessors
- Gap
  - formal assessment of formulating optimization problems with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 uncharted
  - also capabilities/limitations of smaller LLM Llama-2-7b when fine-tuned
- Contributions
  - comprehensive analysis of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2-7b on the task
  - zero-shot and one-shot evaluation: impact of few-shot prompt engineering, learning adaptations
  - empirical study on NL4Opt dataset (cite): GPT-4 best, then GPT-3.5
  - LM4OPT framework to fine-tune Llama-2-7b: significant performance gains

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Many practical challenges from different domains like operations, economics, engineering and computer science can be expressed as optimization problems. Standard optimization algorithms such as the simplex and interior-point methods can solve these problems efficiently. But translating a real-world situation into a mathematical formulation needs specialized knowledge. Because of this expertise barrier many people do not use optimization algorithms, even when these could improve their operations a lot. Automating problem formulation, which means translating natural language descriptions into decision variables, constraints and objective functions, could make these processes accessible to people beyond just operations research experts. So optimization modeling would become accessible to people who cannot afford experts and want to use optimization techniques to increase efficiency. If the problem is formulated correctly, it can easily be solved by transcribing it into an algebraic modeling language that solvers can interpret.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a strong avenue for making optimization problem formulation more accessible and efficient. NLP has made transformative progress over the years, from the beginning of word embeddings to the evolution of language models. Especially since pre-trained language models appeared, these models have reached state-of-the-art results on many NLP tasks, like natural language inference (NLI), question answering, summarization, collaborative writing, etc., with very little task-specific fine-tuning. Recent advances in LLMs, including GPT and Llama, have changed the NLP landscape and practices significantly. These LLMs have parameter sizes of more than several billions, even hundreds of billions, and they have shown remarkable generalization abilities in zero-shot and few-shot settings through prompting. These LLMs have also shown exceptional fine-tuning capabilities, even when fine-tuned on datasets that are much smaller than the ones used by their predecessors.

- Gap
  - formal assessment of formulating optimization problems with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 uncharted
  - also capabilities/limitations of smaller LLM Llama-2-7b when fine-tuned
- Contributions
  - comprehensive analysis of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2-7b on the task
  - zero-shot and one-shot evaluation: impact of few-shot prompt engineering, learning adaptations
  - empirical study on NL4Opt dataset (cite): GPT-4 best, then GPT-3.5
  - LM4OPT framework to fine-tune Llama-2-7b: significant performance gains

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Many practical challenges from different domains like operations, economics, engineering and computer science can be expressed as optimization problems. Standard optimization algorithms such as the simplex and interior-point methods can solve these problems efficiently. But translating a real-world situation into a mathematical formulation needs specialized knowledge. Because of this expertise barrier many people do not use optimization algorithms, even when these could improve their operations a lot. Automating problem formulation, which means translating natural language descriptions into decision variables, constraints and objective functions, could make these processes accessible to people beyond just operations research experts. So optimization modeling would become accessible to people who cannot afford experts and want to use optimization techniques to increase efficiency. If the problem is formulated correctly, it can easily be solved by transcribing it into an algebraic modeling language that solvers can interpret.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a strong avenue for making optimization problem formulation more accessible and efficient. NLP has made transformative progress over the years, from the beginning of word embeddings to the evolution of language models. Especially since pre-trained language models appeared, these models have reached state-of-the-art results on many NLP tasks, like natural language inference (NLI), question answering, summarization, collaborative writing, etc., with very little task-specific fine-tuning. Recent advances in LLMs, including GPT and Llama, have changed the NLP landscape and practices significantly. These LLMs have parameter sizes of more than several billions, even hundreds of billions, and they have shown remarkable generalization abilities in zero-shot and few-shot settings through prompting. These LLMs have also shown exceptional fine-tuning capabilities, even when fine-tuned on datasets that are much smaller than the ones used by their predecessors.

There has not been a formal assessment of this specific task, mathematical formulation of optimization problems from natural language descriptions, using the latest GPT series models, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, which are widely recognized. This research also wants to investigate what a smaller Large Language Model (LLM), Llama-2-7b, can and cannot do when it is fine-tuned on this task. This study has the following contributions:

- Comprehensive analysis of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Llama-2-7b in mathematical formulation of optimization problems from natural language description.

- Evaluation in zero-shot and one-shot settings to understand how few-shot prompt engineering and learning adaptations of the models affect results.

- Empirical study using the NL4Opt dataset, which shows that GPT-4 performs best, followed by GPT-3.5.

- Exploration of using the LM4OPT framework to fine-tune Llama-2-7b, which shows significant performance improvements.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Numerous practical challenges originating from diverse domains such as operations, economics, engineering, and computer science can be articulated as optimization problems [1]. Standard optimization algorithms, including the simplex [2] and interior-point methods [3], can efficiently address these problems. However, translating a real-world situation into a mathematical formulation requires specialized knowledge. This expertise barrier prevents many individuals from utilizing optimization algorithms, even when these could substantially improve their operations. Automating problem formulation, which involves translating natural language descriptions into decision variables, constraints, and objective functions, has the potential to make these processes accessible to individuals beyond operations research experts. Consequently, optimization modeling would become accessible to those who cannot afford experts to improve efficiency using optimization techniques. Provided the problem is correctly formulated, it can be readily solved by transcribing it into an algebraic modeling language interpretable by solvers [4].

Natural Language Processing (NLP) presents a potent avenue for enhancing the accessibility and efficiency of optimization problem formulation. From the inception of word embeddings to the evolution of language models, NLP has undergone transformative progress over the years. Especially with the emergence of pre-trained language models [5], these models have attained state-of-the-art results on a multitude of NLP tasks such as natural language inference (NLI), question answering, summarization, collaborative writing, etc., with minimal task-specific fine-tuning [6]. Recent advancements in LLMs, including GPT [7] and Llama [8], have significantly reshaped NLP landscape and practices. These LLMs, with parameter sizes exceeding several billions and even reaching hundreds of billions, have exhibited remarkable generalization abilities in zero-shot and few-shot settings through prompting. Furthermore, they have shown exceptional fine-tuning capabilities, even when fine-tuned on datasets significantly smaller than those used by their predecessors.

To this end, formal assessment of this specific task - mathematical formulation of optimization problems from natural language descriptions - using the latest GPT series models, namely GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, which have gained widespread recognition, remains uncharted territory. Additionally, this research investigates the capabilities and limitations of a smaller Large Language Model (LLM), Llama-2-7b, when fine-tuned on this task. Consequently, this study offers the following contributions:

- Comprehensive analysis of GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Llama-2-7b in mathematical formulation of optimization problems from natural language description.

- Evaluation in zero-shot and one-shot settings to understand the impact of few-shot prompt engineering and learning adaptations of the models.

- Empirical study using the NL4Opt [4] dataset, demonstrating the superior performance of GPT-4, followed by GPT-3.5.

- Exploration of utilizing the LM4OPT framework to fine-tune Llama-2-7b, revealing significant performance improvements.
